They heard a strange noise and investigated and found a canoe at the water's edge with a strange symbol painted on it.  They felt sure it was a sign of evil and they should not investigate further, but they were curious and they climbed in.  The canoe was from the land of the Dead, and the symbol was a warning to the living.  The men began to row and soon they were surrounded by fog and the land disappeared from sight.  They heard voices calling to them and saw lights around them.  They were in the land of the dead where the dead men's spirits come to hunt for living men to kill.  The men saw a strange city with towering walls and gates, and the spirits appeared.  They saw their own spirits and knew they were doomed.  They were taken to a place of judgment and put on trial for their lives.  The spirits judged them and found them worthy of death because they had gone into the land of the dead.  They were killed and their spirits joined the dead.  The spirits took their bodies back to their village and they were never seen again.  From that day on, the people of Egulac never went into the valley where the dead men's spirits lived.

They painted their faces and bodies as the sorcerer had shown them and were able to hunt whatever they wanted. They kept the source of their power a secret.

The two young men were the originators of the Tlingit potlatch and the Haida potlatch. Their people adopted these practices and they spread to other tribes as well.

They went to the place where the sea monster was known to live, and after a long and difficult hunt, they killed the sea monster and returned to their camp triumphantly carrying the head of the sea monster.  The tribe was very happy and they made merry for many days.  The two young men who had heard the voice were praised for having given the tribe the opportunity to kill the sea monster.

In the fog and the calm of the river,
Where the waves seldom make a sound,
The Raven calls to his servants,
With a voice that is rarely found.

With a voice that is soft and clear,
He calls to them with his eyesight,
That pierces through the fog and fear.

That he offers to those he chooses,
He calls to them with his endless health,
That he shares with those who use.

He calls to them with a task to do,
That is given to them with care,
He calls to them with a promise true,
That they will be his servants fair.

So come now, my servants, he'd say,
And join me in my grand design,
I'll give you wealth and endless day,
And make your spirits rise and shine.

To serve him for all of their days,

He told them that he wanted to adopt them as his sons, and he made them a present of a horse and a gun. They accepted his gift, and he gave them other gifts as well. They stayed with him for a while, and then they returned to their people.

Gootliks was a real person, a chief of the Tlingit people who lived along the coast of British Columbia and Alaska. He was the son of the chief of the Taku River tribe, and he became the chief of the Kasaan tribe on Prince of Wales Island. He was a great chief, and he was a great hunter. He was said to have killed a great number of bears with his bow and arrow.

The story of Gootliks and his adopting the two young men is told in many variations. It was a common theme in the oral literature of the Northwest Coast.

The two young men were afraid, but the woman befriended them and welcomed them to the tribe of the Dead. The man then gave them some advice. He told them that the world was changing and that they would have to go inland to escape the coming great flood. He told them to build their house on a high place and to make it of the sun, the fire, and the eagle. He told them to store their food in the upper part of their house and to keep their minds on the sun and the eagle, and not to look down to the water. They built their house on a hill near a large cedar tree and made it of the sun, the fire, and the eagle. They stored their food in the upper part of their house and kept their minds on the sun and the eagle, as the great hunter and killer had told them to do.

The men were terrified and tried to run but the serpent blocked their way. 

The serpent spoke to them, and asked why they had come to this place. The men explained that they were from Egulac and had come to hunt seals. The serpent explained that he was the guardian of the river and the seals were his brothers. The men agreed and went back to their village and told everyone what had happened. From that day on, the men of Egulac only hunted the seals from a safe distance.

The tale of the sea serpent is a common one among the indigenous peoples of the northwest Pacific coast of North America. It has been told by the Tlingit, Haida, Tsimshian, Kwakiutl, and other tribes. It is a reminder that all living things are connected and that the natural world has a spirit and must be respected.

The "Half-human, Half-frog" was known as Kulkulkan, the feathered serpent, and was the creator deity of the K'iche' people. The K'iche' were the people to whom the young hunters belonged and who were to return to their ancestral homeland. The prophecy was that a 'Half-human, Half-frog' would help them in their return. The 'Half-human, Half-frog' was Quetzalcoatl, the feathered serpent god of the Aztecs and Mayans.

The return of the K'iche' people refers to the return of the Maya civilization to the city of Tikal and other cities in the region. This return was led by two brothers, Tecun Uman and Siyah K'ak', who were the descendants of the ancient Maya nobility. They were from the city of Paynab in the Kuchumatan highlands. The brothers were followed by their people and they established their capital at Tikal. Tecun Uman was the first of a line of sacred kings who were to rule at Tikal. He was followed by his brother Siyah K'ak' and then by their nephew Yax Nuun Ayiin. The return of the K'iche' people to Tikal was in approximately 378 AD.

The next day they went to the place where they had heard and seen the canoes, and found a great number of white men lying around on the beach, some of whom were dead. The young men were horrified at the sight, and went away to tell their people what had happened.

The young men went back to their people, and told them as they had been instructed. The people were afraid to go to that place, and the story was passed from one generation to another.

The canoe came alongside theirs and one of the young men went aboard the other canoe. When he had been there a short time, the canoe began to rock and tip over.  The young man shouted to his companions in the other canoe to help him. They threw him a line and he held on to it. When he was completely at their mercy, they told him that they were members of the tribe of Egulac and that they had come down the river to capture young men for their women.  They took the young man back to their village, where he was made to work in the coal mines until he succeeded in escaping.

Furthermore, The young man was in fact named Handsome Lake, the son of Chief of the Tribe. He was captured by the Egulac tribe, and was made to work in the coal mines, as they traditionally did not do this work. He escaped after some time and returned to his tribe, where he became a chief himself. He later had a vision in which he was told to establish a new religion among his people. This new religion was to be based on the teachings of the Christian missionaries he had met while in captivity, combined with the traditional beliefs of his own people. The religion was to be known as the Longhouse religion.

They heard the sound of a canoe approaching. They called out to the canoeists in the fog, but received no answer.  They heard the canoe touch the shore and then saw a light.  They approached the canoe and found three men inside, freezing and near death from the cold.  They took the three men into their camp and revived them.  The next morning the three men paid for their keep with beads and cloth and went on their way.  The young men from Egulac then took the canoe and went to trade at the Hudson's Bay Company post at York Factory.  On the way they stopped at the Naskapi village of Mingan and traded some of their goods for food.  When they arrived at York Factory they were greeted with great friendliness and were invited to trade there.  They traded some of their beads, furs, and cloth for small goods such as knives, needles, and tobacco.  They then went to Charlton Island and traded at other posts along the way back to their village.

This story is part of a larger collection of folklore stories that were recorded by James S. Durie in the 1930s.  The stories were told to Durie by an unnamed informant who was a Cree from the area of the Moose Cree Reserve in Ontario.  The informant stated that the story was told to him by an old Naskapi man who had lived through the events in the story.  The story is a good example of the way that oral tradition can be used to explain why certain customs and practices exist in the present.  In this case, the custom is trading with the Hudson's Bay Company.  The story explains that trading with the HBC was an old tradition that had been passed down from generation to generation.  It also explains that the Naskapi were not always the only inhabitants of their territory.  They had to share the land with other groups, including the Montagnais, and they had to trade with the HBC in order to get the goods they needed to survive.  The story also shows that the Naskapi were not completely isolated from the rest of the world.  They knew about the fog that was caused by the meeting of warm and cold air masses, and they knew about the Northwest Company which was a rival of the HBC.

The two men went to investigate and found that Natalee was trapped in a cave under the water. They tried to save her but failed. When the tide went out they saw that the cave was part of a larger sea cave. They reported the incident to the chief, and a decision was made to build a wooden causeway to the cave mouth to prevent accidents like this from happening in the future.

The story becomes part of the tribe's oral tradition

The two young men were terrified and ran to their canoes to escape. One of them was a good paddler and got away, but the other was not, and the Thunderbird dived again and again to capsize his canoe and kill him. The young man cried out to the Thunderbird, "Why do you wish to kill me?" The Thunderbird replied, "I do not wish to kill you. If you can answer three questions I will leave you alone." The young man thought for a moment, and then said, "I will answer your questions if you will let me go free." The Thunderbird agreed.

The first question was, "What touches the earth and is always wet, but cannot be seen?" The young man thought for a long time, paddling as he thought. He paddled to the north, and then to the south, and then to the east, and then to the west. Finally, he answered, "The answer is, dew." But the Thunderbird said, "That is not the correct answer. You have cheated, for you thought for a long time and paddled in all directions."

The young man was afraid, for he knew that he would be killed. Then he thought of another answer, and said, "The answer is, a dead man." But the Thunderbird said, "That is not the correct answer."

The young man thought again, and said, "The answer is, a rainbow." And the Thunderbird said, "You are right. You have answered well. I will not kill you. But you must go back to your people and tell them what you have seen, and they will know that you are a wise man."

They heard a strange sound and one young man said to the other, "I wonder what that sound is." The other young man said, "It must be a sea monster." They looked at each other and then they saw a head and two horns and it was a sea monster. The young men ran away and climbed up a tree. The monster came to the tree and the young men looked down at it and one young man said, "Do you know what the monster is doing?" The other young man said, "I think it is eating the roots of the tree." The monster then went away. The young men came down from the tree and went home. The next day they went to the chief and told him what had happened and the chief said, "That was not a monster. That was only a deer going to the water to drink."

Analysis
This story is another example of how the natives of the Pacific Northwest would explain natural phenomena as supernatural events. In this case, the foggy weather may have obscured their view of the deer, and its snorts or grunts may have sounded like a monster to the two young men. In the morning, when the fog had lifted and they knew it was a deer, they attempted to explain away their earlier fear as a misunderstanding.

Variants
This story is told in many variations. In some, the two young men are out hunting and come across a strange sound. They investigate and see a sea monster. They run away and climb a tree. From the tree, they watch the monster eat the roots of a tree. In other versions, the monster is described as having only one horn. In still other versions, the monster is described as having a large head and neck, long ears, and a large tail. In these versions, the two young men watch the monster drink from a river. In all versions, the monster is not considered to be a dangerous creature.

Suddenly they heard a great disturbance at the other end of the river and many voices shouting. They went to see what was happening and discovered that the HBC post at Fort Camos had burned down. The two young men then decided to paddle up river to see if they could help. They arrived at the fort just after the Governor and his party had left for the safety of Fort Nisqually. They found that everyone else had also left except for a young French Canadian man who was lame and could not travel. Together the two young men and the French Canadian decided to rebuild the fort. They worked through the night and by morning the stockade had been rebuilt and the Governor and his party returned to find the fort now secure. The young men were rewarded for their efforts and became good friends with the Governor.

Characters
In this story we have two unnamed young men from Egulac, a French Canadian man and the Governor.

Egulac
Egulac is a village on the south shore of the Strait of Juan de Fuca at the site of present day Port Renfrew, British Columbia. It was an important village for the Straits Salish peoples and was visited by the HBC frequently.

Fort Camos
Fort Camos was a Hudson's Bay Company fur trading post built in 1845. It was located near present day Brentwood Bay on the north shore of the Strait of Juan de Fuca. The fort was abandoned in 1851 and rebuilt in 1853. In 1854 the fort burned down and was rebuilt for a third time.

Fort Nisqually
Fort Nisqually was a Hudson's Bay Company fur trading post built in 1833. It was located near present day Olympia, Washington.

The Story
The story begins with two young men from Egulac going down to the river to hunt seals. They are joined by a French Canadian man who is lame and cannot travel. While they are there a disturbance occurs at the HBC post at Fort Camos and they go to help. They find that everyone else has left and the fort is on fire. The three of them work through the night to rebuild the fort and are rewarded for their efforts.

They heard a strange sound and one of them said it was the sound of people crying. They went to the source of the sound and saw a light. They approached the light and saw a woman sitting in the lotus position with a baby in her arms. She was singing a mournful song. The two young men were very moved and one of them said to the woman "What is the matter? Why are you crying?" The woman told them that she was a sea goddess and that her child was being taken from her and she was crying. She asked them to take her child away from her and bring her back when he was grown up so that she could teach him to be a great chief. The two young men took the child away from her and raised him as their own. When he grew up they took him to the sea goddess and she taught him the secrets of the sea and he became a great chief.

The legend continues that the sea goddess gave the young men a box and told them that whenever they were in trouble they could look into the box and she would help them. She also told them that whenever they looked into the box they would see her face and be reminded of her. The two young men became rich and famous and their descendants became the chiefs of the tribe. They always remembered the sea goddess and her box and looked into it whenever they were in trouble.

This legend is told in a book called "Myths and Legends of Canada" by Robert J. W. McDougall. He says that it is a variation of a legend told by many Native American tribes. He says that the story is told to explain the origin of the chiefs of the tribe and to explain why the sea is so bountiful to the tribe.

They went back to their village and told the others about the Windigo and the pot of stew.  The chief decided that they should go back to the spot where the Windigo had left the stew and offer some of it to the Windigo in order to appease him.  The men went back to the spot and left some of the stew for the Windigo.  The Windigo was pleased with this offering and left them alone.

In popular culture
The story of the Windigo has been popularized by Richard Wagamese in his novel, "Ragged Company".  In the novel, the Windigo is depicted as a malevolent spirit that preys on those who are lost in the wilderness.  The story has also been retold in graphic novel format by artist David Alexander.

This is a story from the Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka) tribe from the Pacific Northwest.  The Nuu-chah-nulth people believe that the whale is a spirit being and that it provides them with protection and food.  The tribe respects the whale and its spirit and does not hunt it without a good reason and with the proper respect.
The story also illustrates a theme that is common in native mythology where the natural world has a spirit and is alive.  The story also illustrates the consequences of not respecting these spirits.

In reality
The story is a retelling of an event that took place in 1884, near the village of Egulac (now Bella Bella) on the central coast of British Columbia, Canada. The two young men were William Hind and Frank Quimp. They were out hunting for seals when they encountered a sea monster, which was actually a killer whale. A local native, Tateek, told them that the sea monster was the spirit of a man who had been killed by a rival tribe, and that it could be appeased by offering gifts. They returned to the village and told the others what had happened. The chief, or 'Hereditary Chief' in the local custom, decided that the two young men should try to appease the killer whale by throwing gifts into the water. The two young men rowed out to the killer whale in a canoe and threw gifts into the water. The killer whale did not attack them and swam away. The two young men were hailed as heroes and were given great honor.

While they were sitting in their canoe they heard Owl, in the forest, calling to Raven.  Owl was saying: "I see you, Raven, I see you."  And Raven replied: "I know, I know, you are the only one who sees me."  The two young men listened in astonishment as Owl and Raven conversed back and forth for some time.
Then Raven said to Owl: "I am going to tell you a secret.  I can change into a human being and I can change others into human beings too.  But if I change you into a human being, you will be trapped in that human body and you will never be able to change back again."  And Owl said: "I know, I know, you are the trickster, Raven."  And Raven said: "I am going to change you now, into a human being."  And in an instant, Owl was transformed into a man.  And Raven said: "Now you must live as a human being, and you will never be able to change back again."  And Owl became very sad, for he knew that he would never again be able to fly up into the sky as an owl.  And Raven said: "I am going to change you back now."  And in an instant, Owl was changed back into an owl.  And Owl flew up into the sky, and Raven laughed and laughed, for he knew that he had tricked Owl.
And the two young men listened to Raven's laughter until it echoed through the forest and then they returned to their camp.

Interpretation
The story illustrates the importance of social order in the indigenous communities of the Northwest Coast. It also shows the consequences of breaking the law and the importance of following the rules in order to maintain social harmony.

They heard a strange sound and one of them said that it was the sound of a great many people praying. The other man agreed with him and they both listened for some time. Then they heard the sound of a canoe approaching. They called out and asked who it was that was coming. An old man called out and said it was him. When he came close enough they could see him, they recognized him as the chief of all the Indians in that country. He told them that he had been watching them for some time and that they must be good and true men if they wished to prosper in that country. After talking with him for some time, the old chief went away and left them. From that day on they prospered and were always successful in all their attempts.

Interpretation
The story of the two young men from Egulac who heard the sound of many people praying and then met the old chief, represents the coming together of two cultures: the Indian (Egulac) and the European (the two young men). The old chief represents the spirit of the land, guiding the newcomers and helping them prosper.

The tale of the Friendly Giant
According to the tale, the creature was a giant who lived in the waters of the inlet. He was originally feared by the people of Egulac because it was believed that the giant caused the fog and calm that sometimes came over the inlet which made it difficult for the Tlingit people to hunt for food in the water. The giant was a solitary creature and was avoided by the people of Egulac because of this. However, as the legend goes, two young men from the village went down to the inlet to hunt seals and befriended the giant. The giant was a gentle creature and was just lonely. After this encounter, the people of Egulac welcomed the giant into their village and it became a part of their community. From that time, the giant became a protector of the village and its people and was no longer a source of fear.

Variations of the tale
The tale of the friendly giant is a common one among the Tlingit people of the Northwest Coast of North America. Variations of the tale have been reported among the Tlingit people of Kake, Angoon, and Sitka. In some versions of the tale, the creature is described as a whale and in others it is described as a giant octopus. In some versions, the creature is described as being friendly from the beginning and is not feared by the people of the village.

Suddenly they heard a great booming sound right in front of them, and a great big shape rose up out of the water.  It was the great Thunderbird coming to earth to hunt the people because he was angry.  The young men were so frightened they ran for their canoes and paddled as fast as they could back to their camp on the shore. The wall was many feet high and many feet thick, and it took many men many days to build it.  The Thunderbird came back to the lake to hunt the people, but when he saw the great wall he could not get over it, and he became very angry.  He flew around the lake in great sweeps, smashing his mighty wings against the wall and shaking the ground with each beat of his great wings, but he could not get over the wall.  The people were safe.  The two young men who had first heard the Thunderbird and had run away were very ashamed, and they felt that they must make amends to their fellow villagers for their fright.  So they decided to go back to the place where they had first heard the Thunderbird's great booming call, and they built a great big fire and danced all night long to drive the Thunderbird away.  And from that day on, the Thunderbird did not come back to their lake to hunt the people.

They swam to the shore and looked back and saw a tremendous steam-powered CPR ship passing by.  They realized that the fog was a fog bank caused by the steam from the ship's funnel.  The two young men decided that they would go to school to learn how to build ships like that, and so they went to Victoria, British Columbia, and enrolled in the British Columbia Collegiate Institute, which later became the University of British Columbia.  They became architects and built many structures in the city of Vancouver, but they never forgot their adventure in Egulac and the ship that caused it.

The tale of the two young men is a recurring theme in British Columbia history. It was told as a cautionary tale about the dangers of fog and the importance of learning new skills. It was also used to explain why the University of British Columbia was founded. The story has been retold many times with different details. In one version the two young men were students at the University of Washington, in another they were students at the University of British Columbia. In most versions the men were not from Egulac but from the Haida Gwaii. In one version the ship that caused the fog was a British ship, in another it was a Canadian ship. The story was used to explain why the university was moved from Victoria to Vancouver, in another version the two men were inspired by the ship to become architects and build a university. The story was first told in 1897, in a speech by the Minister of Lands and Works in the British Columbia legislature. It was first published in 1914 in "Old-time stories of Vancouver" by Frank Appleton.

The Great Flood is a common motif in the oral traditions of the indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest.  The story above is a version told by the Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka) people.
There are many variations of the Great Flood story told by the indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest.  Some of the variations include:

The Tlingit people say that Raven, the culture hero, caused the flood.  He had been tricked by the Frog and his wife, who had turned into the sun and the moon, and had his head crushed.  Raven caused the flood to wash away the people who had caused his troubles.

The Haida people say that the Great Flood was caused by the Earth shaker, a giant octopus who lived in the deep ocean.  He caused the ocean to rise up and flood the land.

The Kwakwaka'wakw people say that the Great Flood was caused by a giant eagle who destroyed the first world, created by the Raven.

The Salish peoples say that the Great Flood was caused by a giant water monster that was angered by the people's disrespect for the land and their refusal to share.  The hero of the story is Coyote, who tricks the water monster and causes the flood to recede.

The story of the Great Flood is told by many other tribes, including the Bella Coola, Bella Bella, and the Sto:lo.

He said to the two young men, "What do you want?" They said, "We want to kill seals and trade pelts with you." The Sauk said, "I want to give you a gift. I will give you a magic root that will enable you to kill buffalo easily. But you must promise me that you will use it only for a good purpose." They agreed. The Sauk gave them a root and left.
The two young men of the Egulac returned to their people and became rich and prosperous because of the magic root. They used it only to kill buffalo for food and hides. But their descendants became greedy and used it to kill buffalo for beaver pelts.
Then the buffalo herds disappeared. The two young men of the Egulac saw this and were sad, because they knew that their people would suffer. They went to the place where they had seen the Sauk and called upon him to help them. The Sauk appeared and said, "You have broken the contract we made. You have used the magic root for an evil purpose. The buffalo can no longer be killed so easily. You must now learn to live as I do, by hunting only for food and giving thanks to the Great Spirit for the gift of life."

They heard a great commotion up the river and saw a canoe coming towards them.  They heard the people in the canoe singing and laughing.  The canoe came alongside their own canoe and they saw that it was filled with women.  The women had long black hair which hung down and covered their breasts.  The women sang a song and then gave the men gifts of tobacco and of their own hair.  The men were surprised and happy.  The women then sang another song and climbed back into their canoe which turned into a mermaid and dived into the water.  The two young men watched as the mermaid canoe disappeared into the foggy night.  The men then continued their journey down the river.

Interpretation
This legend can be interpreted as the story of a transformative journey.  The two young men are on a journey down the river of life when they encounter the mermaids.  The mermaids represent the transformative power of women and the feminine.  The tobacco and hair are symbols of this transformative power.  The mermaids are not evil but represent the mysteries of life and death.  The men are transformed by their encounter and continue their journey down the river of life.

During the ceremony, the young man's grandfather went into a trance and spoke to the Fog People.  He asked them to release his grandson.  The Fog People agreed and the young man was released.  From that day on, the tribe made offerings to the Fog People whenever they went into the fog.  They also began to honor the Fog People as protectors instead of enemies.

Variations
This myth is told among the Nuu-chah-nulth peoples of the Pacific Northwest.  It is told with slight variations depending on the tribe.  In some stories, the young men are not out hunting, but are on a mission to retrieve a stolen potlatch gift.  In other stories, the young men are not from Egulac, but from another Nuu-chah-nulth tribe.  In still other stories, the young men are not captured, but instead outsmart the Fog People.  Despite these variations, the basic story remains the same.

The young men from Egulac approached and were invited to help set up the teepee.  They were then invited inside to eat and to stay for the night.  The men inside were traders from the Hudson's Bay Company.  They traded tobacco and rum for furs and then the traders left in the morning.  The two young men from Egulac returned to their camp and related what had happened.  They decided to go to the fort to see if they could learn the ways of trading and become rich like the men they had met.

The two young men from Egulac reached the Hudson's Bay Company fort on the Saskatchewan River and befriended a Cree trader named Ne-go-shus. Ne-go-shus taught them the ways of the fur trade, and in time they became skilled traders. They built a log cabin near the present site of Portage la Prairie.
The two men decided to become partners in the fur trade and established a trading post at the junction of the Assiniboine and Red Rivers. They called their post Fort Bourbon since they took brandy as payment for furs. They were the first of what became a long line of whiskey traders along the western fur trade routes.

The two men became wealthy and powerful in the fur trade. They were also instrumental in the establishment of the Selkirk Colony, which eventually led to the creation of the Province of Manitoba. The mythology of the Tlingit people
The Tlingit people are a group of Native Americans who live in the North Pacific in what is now the United States and Canada. They tell many stories about the world and the beings who inhabit it. This story is about the spirit of the middle class.

The story of the woman and the two hunters
In this story, the woman is a supernatural being who comes to claim one of the two hunters who are out hunting seals. She does this by making a strange sound which frightens the men. They both shoot arrows into the fog, and when the woman touches one of the men with her arrow, he falls down. She takes him to her house and treats him well. The man is grateful for her kindness and gives her many gifts. In the end, the woman sets the man free and he returns to his village.

The idea of the middle class
The concept of the middle class is a social and economic category that refers to people who are not poor and not rich. They have a moderate amount of wealth and resources and are considered to be part of the mainstream of society. In this story, the woman represents the middle class and is a supernatural being who comes to claim one of the hunters. She is described as the spirit of the middle class.

Suddenly they heard a great booming sound and a wave lifted them up and carried them inland. They were deposited at the spot where the village of Tofino now stands.  They decided that this place was safe from the enemies of their people and decided to settle there.  They built a palisade for protection and the village grew.  The name Tofino comes from the name of the chief who ruled there.  Tofino was the son of a chief from the Nootka Sound area and a matrilineal chief from the Egmont area.

The story continues with the arrival of the Spanish.  The Spanish arrived in 1792, and a trading post was set up at the village site.  The villagers traded with the Spanish for beads, knives, and other small items.  The Spanish also introduced the villagers to the horse.  The villagers traded with the Spanish until 1810 when the fur trade opened up and the Spanish trading post closed.

The first Europeans to live among the people of Tofino were the Nuu-chah-nulth and Spanish interpreters, Father Francisco de la Costa and his servant Esteban. They arrived in 1792 and remained for a short time. The Spanish returned in 1803 when a smallpox epidemic was sweeping through the region. Father Francisco and Esteban helped the villagers through this crisis and were well regarded by the people.
Father Francisco returned to Tofino in 1808, and it was here that he died.

The first non-native settlers arrived in the 1860s. The village became a trading post for sealskins and later salmon. In 1889, a smallpox epidemic swept through the village and many Nuu-chah-nulth died. The village was largely abandoned and the people moved to villages further north where they were safer from disease.

In 1900, a group of loggers came to the area and established a logging camp. The loggers had to leave when the timber was exhausted, but they had started a tradition of logging in the area. Logging continued until the 1950s when it became uneconomical to log on the rugged coast.

While they were sitting in their canoe they heard a supernatural being approaching in the mist. The being stepped into the canoe with them and spoke to them. The young men were terrified but the being told them not to be afraid. He told them that he was a spirit of the place and that he would help them if they needed it, but that he would also kill them if they broke the laws of the land. The young men were so shaken by this encounter that they paddled back to their village immediately. They told their chief and the other villagers what had happened and the chief told them that the spirit was the guardian of the land and that they must respect it if they wanted to live in the village. From that day on, the villagers tried to live in harmony with the spirit.

This story is typical of the many encounters that indigenous people of the Pacific Northwest had with supernatural beings. These beings were often seen as guardians of the land or water and were usually treated with respect. The people believed that they could help the tribe in times of need or punish them if they broke the laws of the land.

The story is retold in the book "Longhouse of the Seven Sisters" by Robert J. Miller.

Suddenly they heard a great swishing sound and saw a great fish leap out of the water and land on the bank beside them.  It was a Steller's sea-cow, a fish-eating marine mammal.  The two young men were terrified and ran back to their village.  They reported what had happened to the chief, and the chief decided to send a party to kill the fish.  They went back to the river and killed the fish, and took its tongue home to their village.  They put the tongue in a pot, and set it over the fire to cook.  While the tongue was cooking, the young men began to feel very hungry.  They looked in the pot and saw that the tongue was shrinking and shrinking until it was very small.  They looked at each other and said: "Now we know why the Steller's sea-cow is called a 'giant' fish; its tongue is very tasty but very small."  They cut the tongue into small pieces and put the pieces into a basket to take home.  But the pieces grew larger and larger until the basket was full and very heavy.  They carried the basket home to their families and friends, and they all ate the sea-cow tongue until they were full.  Then they went to sleep.  The next morning the two young men went to the place where they had killed the sea-cow and found that it had grown back again and was lying in the water.  They went back to their village and told their friends and families what had happened, and they all went back to the river to hunt seals and to eat sea-cow tongue.

A canoe carrying three men from the village of Fort Simpson approached. The canoe was headed for Egulac. In the canoe were Chief Cus, his son, and his brother. The chief and his companions were able to tie up their canoe beside the one the attackers were in and took the wounded man hostage.  The chief then went to the village and spoke with the head chief, explaining what had happened.  The head chief decided that since the attackers had been the ones to initiate the fight, that the chief and his companions had the right to take their weapons and some trade goods as compensation for the attack.  The chief and his companions then sailed to York Factory to complete their trading mission.

Interpretation
This story is an example of a vision quest. The young men are seeking spiritual power. They go to the place where they believe the spirits live and they receive visions or dreams from the spirits. They learn things that they can use to help their tribe or clan. The young men are seeking knowledge that will help them survive and thrive. The young men are also seeking to connect with their ancestors and to understand their place in the universe.

This is a traditional story from the Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka) First Nation of Vancouver Island.  It is one of many stories explaining the phenomena of fog banks that form on the coast of Vancouver Island.  The Nuu-chah-nulth people have a great respect for the sea and all its creatures.  They believe that the sea provides for them and they must in turn provide for the sea.  This story is also an explanation of why the Nuu-chah-nulth people have a great respect for the potlatch ceremony and the giving of gifts.  The potlatch is a time of celebration and giving and is a way of renewing relationships and strengthening the community.

The older man called out again, "Who are you?" and the voice replied, "I am the Windigo, the Great Spirit of the Air, the Master of the Fog." The older man was not afraid and said, "What do you want of us?" The Windigo replied, "I have been waiting for you, my children. I have watched you from afar and I have chosen you to be my friends and my messengers."

The two men were amazed and asked, "What must we do?" The Windigo said, "I will give you great power and knowledge. In return, you will do my bidding and will help me to destroy those who oppose me." The older man was tempted, but the younger man was afraid and begged them to leave. The older man agreed and the two men left the place of the Windigo and returned to their people.

After a while, the older man fell ill and was possessed by the Windigo. He became cruel and evil and destroyed everything in his path. The people were afraid of him and tried to stop him, but he was too powerful. The younger man tried to help the people, but he was too weak. The older man, possessed by the Windigo, destroyed everything in sight.

The younger man realized that the only way to stop the older man was to kill him. He took a poisoned arrow and shot the older man. The older man fell dead and the Windigo left his body and entered the younger man. The people were very afraid, but the younger man was not evil and he used the power of the Windigo to help the people. He became a great leader and helped his people defeat their enemies.

The people were very grateful and built a great temple in the younger man's honor. They offered sacrifices to the Windigo and asked for its help in all their endeavors. The younger man became the new chief and he and the Windigo lived in the great temple. The people were very happy and prospered under the younger man's rule.

They heard a great commotion up the river and saw a great canoe coming towards them. It was canoe of the Hul'q'umi'num people from the north and they were celebrating because they had just killed a grizzly bear.
The two young men from Egulac invited the Hul'q'umi'num people to come to their village for the potlatch they were preparing to give. The Hul'q'umi'num people agreed to come and they went to the village of the Egulac people.
The potlatch was a great success and the Hul'q'umi'num people gave the Egulac people a great gift: a potlatch of copper shields. The copper shields were the insignia of the Hul'q'umi'num people's rank and power, and the bestowal of these shields meant that the people of Egulac were now considered to be of the same rank and power as the people of the north.
The people of Egulac became known as the "people with the copper shields" and their village became an important trading center. The copper used for the shields came from Nanaimo, where the Hul'q'umi'num people went to mine it.
This story illustrates the importance of potlatching and gift-giving in the culture of the First Nations people of the Pacific Northwest Coast. It also illustrates the fact that the potlatch was not just a social event, but had political and economic implications as well.

The story continues:  The young men had been away from their village for many months and when they returned they found that their people had moved to a new village site.  They decided to stay at the seal-hunting place and built a longhouse there.  They hunted for seal in the winter and gathered berries and hunted deer in the summer. The two young men became their leaders and the place became known as the village of Tofino.

They heard a strange sound and one of them said it was the sound of people dancing far away in the forest. The other man said it was the wind blowing through the trees. They went to investigate and came upon a large gathering of people dancing. The strangers were welcomed and invited to join in the dance. After dancing all night, the two men returned to their canoe and went home.

The next day, they went back to the place where they had left their things and found that a strange disease had overcome their people. They were unable to move and were dying. The two men took their things and ran away to the place where they had danced the night before. When they arrived, they saw that their people were also there and that they were not affected by the disease. The two men danced all night and when they stopped to rest, they saw that they were healed.

The men realized that the dance was what healed them and that it was the spirit of the land helping them. From that day on, the two men dedicated their lives to the dance and traveled from place to place teaching it to others. They were known as the "Dancers of the End of the World".

The dance became known as the "Healing Dance" and was used to heal people whenever there was an outbreak of disease. The dance was also used to heal people who were infected with smallpox which was brought to the area by Europeans.

The Healing Dance was also used to heal the land. When the Europeans arrived, they cut down many trees which caused the land to become barren. The Healing Dance was used to heal the land and restore it to its former beauty.

The Healing Dance is still performed today by the Nuu-chah-nulth people.

They asked what had happened, and the two young men said that the whale had burned them up and swallowed them, but that they had escaped by jumping out of its mouth before it could close its jaws.  The people from Egulac knew that this could not be true, for no one had ever escaped from the jaws of Abolhknah.  They knew that the two young men must have been burned by a volcanic eruption, and that they must have been overcome by the fumes and lost their memory, for they could not explain how they had escaped.  The people from Egulac took the two young men back to the village, and they died soon after from their burns.

The people of Egulac told this story to explain the volcanic activity on the coast, and to explain why no one from Egulac ever went down to the river to hunt seals during the winter months.

The next day the fog lifted and the Egulac people saw that the strangers' canoe was from the Nootka Sound area of the Alaskan panhandle. The Egulac people realized that the strangers had come from a place very far away.
The Tles and Tla'las traveled along the coast, trading and making alliances with the different First Nations groups they met. They continued their journey until they found a place to call home. The Tles and Tla'las became the ancestors of the later Tlingit people.

In reality
The ship "Cumberland" was the first American ship to explore the Columbia River in 1824. The ship was under the command of Captain Richard T. Beebe. The natives the crew encountered were from the Wishram band of the Yakama people. The Wishram were friendly to the crew and showed them the area, including the location of the present day Maryhill Museum of Art's stone house. The captain traded some trinkets for furs and beads. The captain was not able to reach the source of the Columbia River and turned back at the Dalles.

In popular culture
The tale of the "Father of all Waters" and the "Fountain of all Rivers" is told in the book "Chinook Legends" by Francis de Boscawen Bardsley. The story is told in the chapter "How the Columbia River was Discovered" and is also recounted in the book "The Columbia River" by Robert M. Kautz. The story is also told in the book "The Spotted Bear" by Mary P. W. Grier.

This story is told in slightly different ways by different First Nations groups in the area.  For the Tlingit, Raven is the culture hero who brought the sun, moon, and stars to the sky. Suddenly a canoe came over the water and landed on the shore.  The men in the canoe were the spirits of the dead who had drowned in the river.  They told the young men to come with them to the land of the dead, where they would be treated well.
The young men refused, so the spirits took them to a meadow where the young men's sweethearts were waiting for them.  The spirits told the young men that they could be with their sweethearts for a short time, but they would never be able to leave the meadow.  The young men decided to stay with their sweethearts, but after a while they grew tired of the meadow and wanted to return to their homes.  The spirits told them that they could leave by running through the trees, so the young men raced through the trees and returned to their homes.
From that day on, the young men were the only people who were able to leave the meadow.  They became the guardians of the spirits and were able to bring back the spirits of the dead to the meadow.  The young men became the new spirits of the dead and were able to visit their families and friends in the night, but they could not leave the meadow.

Suddenly they heard a great uproar and a wave splashed over them.  A great sea monster had come up from the depths.  The young men were frightened, but the monster did not harm them.  Instead, it showed them a cave underwater and told them that when they wished to hunt seals in that place they must call out to the seal people and ask permission.  The monster then went away.  The young men returned to their people and told them what had happened.  From that day on, whenever the people of Egulac went to hunt seals in that place, they called out to the seal people and asked permission.

This story is told in the novel "Trickster" by E. Pauline Johnson.  It is a variation of the story of the Sea Otter and the White Man told by the Nuu-chah-nulth people of the west coast of Vancouver Island.  The story is an example of a treaty story.  It explains the reason for the Nuu-chah-nulth people's respect for the treaties that the Canadian government made with them.  According to the story, the sea monster is a trickster who helps the people by showing them a short cut to the seal rookeries.  The people are grateful and obey the monster's request to ask permission before hunting seals in that place.  The monster is a symbol of the treaties which the Nuu-chah-nulth people saw as a short cut to getting what they needed to live.  They were grateful to the Canadian government for bringing them the gifts of trade and Christianity and obeyed the request to ask permission before taking resources from the land.

The two young men stayed in the cage until the Sasquatch went away and then they escaped. They ran as fast as they could back to the canoe and paddled as fast as they could back to their village.

When they arrived back home they were hailed as heroes and the chief gave the woman's father a great feast in her honor. The young woman was very happy to be home and the two men were honored for their bravery. The story of the brave ones is a common one among the Salish peoples of the Pacific Northwest. It is told by many different tribes with the names of the characters changed to fit the tribe's oral history. The story is told to explain the creation of the Squamish and Tsleil-Waututh First Nations.

The story has been retold in a book by the same name, The Brave Ones, by Robert J. Anderson. The book was published in 2007 by Harbour Publishing.

The legend of the horned devils explains why the winter comes every year. But the Indians also wondered what caused the summer. They believed that in summer the devil went to sleep, and that his wife, the blue jay, kept him warm with her feathers. When the horned devil awakens again, he blows snow from his horns and the winter comes.

The legend of the horned devils is widespread among the indigenous peoples of North America. In some versions, the devils are depicted as white men with horns, in others as monsters with horns and a body like a bison or an elephant. In some versions, the devils are not evil, but are simply the creators of the world and of the seasons.

She invited the two young men to come and live with them, and look upon her and her husband as father and mother, and she said that they would be welcome to come to their camp whenever they pleased.

The two young men accepted her invitation, and went with her to her camp. They found that the people were very kind to them, and treated them as if they were their own sons. The woman's name was Wenjimauk, and her husband's name was Weshkiki. They became very fond of their adopted sons, and gave them the names of Weshkiki and Wenjimauk, and they lived with them for many years.

One day the woman's brother, the chief, came to visit them. He was very pleased with the two young men, and asked them to go with him to the place where the Saskatchewan and South Branch join, and help him to look after his people. They went with him, and remained there some time. While they were there a great smallpox epidemic broke out, and many of the people died. The two young men, however, did not catch the disease, and they helped to nurse those who were sick.

After a while the two young men returned to their adoptive parents, and remained with them until the day when they themselves became the chiefs of their own band.

This story is told by William Apess, an Abenaki from the St. Francis mission in Quebec.  It was collected by David W. Richardson in 1841.

This is a common theme in many Aboriginal cultures.  The spirits of the dead returning to the place of their birth.  In some stories, the spirits come to help the living.  In others, they come to punish the living for some wrong that was committed.  In still other stories, the spirits come to teach the living some important lesson.

In any case, it is important to remember that Aboriginal peoples did not believe that death was the end of life.  Instead, death was just another stage in the cycle of life.  The spirits of the dead continued to live on, even if they were no longer physically present.

They heard a strange sound and investigated and found a canoe beached near the strand line.  In the canoe they saw a woman weeping.  She told them that she was the sister of the Raven and that her brother had caused the fog and calm to happen so that she could meet them and tell them what was going to happen in the world.  She told them of a box that was buried in a certain spot and that when it was found the world would be destroyed.  She also told them that a great flood would come and only those who were in a canoe that was well sealed would survive.  She gave them a hint that the canoe should be built near the dead tree that points to the center of the world.  She also told them that the world would end in a hot day followed by a cold day.

They returned to their village and told their people about the woman and what she had said.  The people decided to prepare for the coming flood by building a large and well-sealed canoe and burying food and supplies in the ground near the dead tree.  When the people had finished their preparations they decided to find the box that was spoken of.  They found it and when they opened it they were attacked by demons.  They fought them off and when they had gone the box began to glow and a light came out of it and filled the sky.  The next day the sun rose and then set and the world went dark and cold and the people were glad that they had listened to the woman and prepared.  The people got into their canoe and rode out the flood.  When the flood had passed the people went to find new land and founded a new village.

The story is found in the stories of the Nuu-chah-nulth people who lived on the west coast of Vancouver Island.  The story has been retold many times with the people finding land on the California coast or on an island in the Pacific Ocean.  The story has also been adapted into a children's story with the people finding land on an island in the Pacific Ocean and the flood being caused by a volcano.

They heard a sound on the water and one of them said that it was probably just a beaver. But the other one said that it was not a beaver, it was something else.  They decided to investigate the sound and went out in their canoe. They heard the sound again and it was near a small island. They landed at the island and went into the bush to investigate. They came upon a large circular structure that was covered with branches and leaves. In the center of the structure was a fire and around the fire were many people who were singing and dancing. The two young men were amazed and watched from a distance.
Suddenly one of the people noticed them and called out to them and asked them to come and join in their dance. The two young men were hesitant but then decided to join in. They were welcomed and were given food and were invited to stay for three days. After three days they returned to their village and told their friends and families about their adventure. From that time on, the young men went regularly to the place of the dance and learned many things from the people who lived there.

Interpretation
The story of the "Circle Dance" is a metaphor for the journey of the human spirit. The two young men represent the individual seeking knowledge and understanding. The circular structure represents the cyclical nature of life, death and rebirth. The fire represents the transformative power of the spirit. The dance represents the connection between all living things and the importance of community and sharing.

Variants
There are many variations of this story throughout North America. Some stories tell of the people being transformed into animals and others tell of the people being taken to the "Land of Souls". All of the stories tell of the importance of the individual journey and the connection to community and spirit.

Suddenly they heard a great noise and the water began to boil.  The young men were frightened and paddled to the shore.  When they looked back, they saw a great water monster rising from the sea.  The monster was so large that its head touched the sky, its eyes were like the sun and moon, and its body was covered with scales as hard as iron.  The monster opened its wide mouth and fire came out.  The young men ran inland and hid.  The monster then went up the river and destroyed all the villages on the banks with fire and water.  The young men watched from their hiding place as the monster destroyed their homes and killed their people.  The monster then left the river and the young men came out from their hiding place to see what was left of their village.  They saw that everything was destroyed and their people were dead.  The young men cried and mourned for their dead.  The monster had come from the sea every year to destroy the village ever since.  The young men made canoes and went to live on the river.  They saw the monster every year but it did not attack them in their canoes.

The young men decided to build a village on the shore of the river and live there.  They built a wall around the village for protection.  The monster came as usual but it could not enter the village because of the wall.  The young men watched the monster as it became smaller and smaller every year.  They realized that the monster was getting old.  They built a great house for the monster and treated the monster with respect.  The monster was happy and stopped destroying their village.  The young men took care of the monster and it took care of them.  The monster was their guardian and protector.  The young men learned that even monsters can be kind and deserve respect.

The story of the water monster is a story that has been passed down from generation to generation among the Tlingit people.  It is a story that teaches that even creatures that seem scary and mean can be kind and deserve respect.  It is a story that teaches that we should not be afraid of things that are different from us and that we should try to understand them instead.  The story of the water monster is a story that teaches that we should try to live in peace with all creatures, big and small, monster or human.

The Potlatch Dance
The Potlatch Dance is a ceremonial dance of the Indigenous peoples of the Northwest Coast of North America. It is given to celebrate important events such as the naming of a child, the installation of a new chief, the opening of a new house or the settling of a debt. It is accompanied by feasting, gift-giving and storytelling.

The Potlatch is not a single dance but a series of dances that can last for several days. The dances are performed by men, women and children and the costumes vary from very simple to very elaborate. The dances are accompanied by drums, rattles and chanting.  The Potlatch ceremony is an important part of the culture of the Indigenous peoples of the Northwest Coast and is a UNESCO Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.

The Potlatch is also the name for the gifts that are given during these ceremonies. The Potlatch dance is a celebration of the traditional culture of the Indigenous peoples of the Northwest Coast and is an important way of preserving and passing on their traditions from one generation to the next.

The Potlatch was banned by the Canadian government in 1885 after the hanging of Louis Riel but the ban was lifted in 1951.  The Potlatch continues to be an important part of the culture of the Indigenous peoples of the Northwest Coast and is celebrated by many Indigenous communities in British Columbia, Washington State, Oregon and California.

The Potlatch Dance is one of the 12 National Treasures of Canada.

They said that they did not know. The HBC then asked them if they had done it. They said that they had. The HBC then asked them if they were going to do it again. They said that they were not. The HBC then asked them if they knew that it was wrong. They said that they did. The HBC then asked them if they would like to work for the HBC. They said that they would. They said that they thought the whale had come in to breathe, but now it was dead they would not know what to do with it.  The old men said that they could not leave it there, but must take it back to the village, and so they did.  The whale was taken back to the village, and they all decided that as it was a gift from the Whale-Folk it must be shared by all.  So they cut it up and gave a share of the meat to every family in the village.  They also gave a share to the two young men who had found it, and after that no one went hunting for seal or meat for three days, for there was enough to feed everyone.  After three days the people went back to their hunting and their fishing, but from that time on they no longer killed whales, for they realized that they were not truly owners of the meat, but only of that which was given to them by the Whale-Folk.

They heard a great commotion up the river and saw a great light. They went towards the light and saw a canoe beaching on the shore. They went towards the canoe and saw a man getting out of the canoe, it was Hiyo'xwa' (the Transformer). He was followed by a man carrying a package. The man who came out of the canoe went into the forest and the man with the package came towards them. He said "I have come to give you a gift" and opened the package and gave them a box. Inside the box was a silver ball. He told them to shake the ball and keep it safe. They did as they were told and the ball became a human child. They named the child Kwaday'da'xw (the Raven). The child grew up and became a great chief and the people who lived there called him Kwaday'da'xw (the Raven).

Interpretation
The story of the Raven is a common one in the mythology of the indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest. In this story, the Raven is a trickster figure who uses his cunning to acquire knowledge, in this case, the sun, moon, and stars. The story also shows the importance of the potlatch ceremony, as the Raven gives the people the gift of knowledge in the form of a potlatch.

Variants
The story of the Raven is told by many different groups in the Pacific Northwest. In some versions, the Raven is transformed from a human into a bird by the Transformer. In other versions, the Raven is already a bird when the Transformer gives him the sun, moon, and stars.

The people in the canoe were the "Tillicum" who came from the land of the dead. The Tillicum told the young men that the world was going to be destroyed and only a few people would survive. Interpretation
The story of the "Tillicum" is a prophecy about a coming destruction. It is not clear if the young men are meant to be the protagonists of the story or if they are just the narrators. The story does not specify what kind of destruction is meant to occur. The story does not seem to be related to the Flood myth found in other Indigenous cultures of the Pacific Northwest. The myth may have been used to explain natural disasters or disasters caused by the actions of humans.

Variants
There are several variants of this story. In one variant, the Tillicum are described as being cannibals who come to eat the living. In another variant, the Tillicum are described as being people who lived in the land of the dead.

Wenut told the young men many things about the natural world and the spirits that lived in the forest, and the young men learned a great deal from her.

The Return Journey
However, the spirits of the forest were not happy with the young men, for they had taken Wenut away from her vision quest.  A great storm arose, and the young men were forced to flee the village.  Wenut decided to go with them, and they set out on the return journey.  The spirits of the forest continued to punish them, and they were forced to face many trials.  Wenut used her knowledge of the natural world to help them, and they were able to survive.  They reached the village of the young men's tribe, and the young men were hailed as heroes for having brought home a chief's daughter.  Wenut decided to stay with the young men, and they lived happily ever after.

The man fell into a trance and saw his father leading him to a great house where there was feasting and celebration. He awoke from his trance to find the raven still perched on his shoulder.
